newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Fear of police soars after Brazil video brutality.
newsitem.headline: Fear of police soars after Brazil video brutality.

text.p: Fear and mistrust of the police has risen sharply in Sao Paulo since a videotape aired this week with shocking images of police violence, according to poll released on Thursday.

The number of people who said they feared the military police more than they trusted them rose to 74 percent from around 50 percent in a similar poll conducted in December 1995, according to the daily Folha de Sao Paulo, which published the survey.

That figure dropped sharply among people who had not seen the videotape, aired on Brazilian television on Monday night. Of those, only 54 percent said they mistrusted the police while 44 percent felt secure.
Human rights groups have condemned the images that showed Sao Paulo police officers torturing and intimidating civilians at a roadblock and allegedly killing a passenger in one car.
Activists said brutality was rampant on the force but officers were rarely punished.
The poll showed mistrust of the police was especially high among blacks -- 83 percent said they lived in fear of the police -- and people who had already been stopped for checks.
The latter group was the most favourable toward the death penalty for the 10 officers arrested in connection with last month's incidents.

The police violence video, which has been shown repeatedly on several channels, has triggered a wave of public outcry against police abuses. Thousands of people have called radio talk shows to express their disgust at the scenes shown on the videotape while many told of their own humiliating experiences at the hands of police officers.
In Brasilia, congress members have reacted by speeding up debate of legislation calling for tougher sentences for police found guilty of torture and extortion.

The Folha de Sao Paulo survey also showed a shift in public perception of the causes of police corruption. In 1995, the public blamed low salaries for most abuses of power, but in 1997 they said lack of training and low recruitment levels were the main causes.
The survey questioned 1,080 people in an unspecified period of time and has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.
